planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring into humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in a sheltered site.

directions: This small Chinese understory tree bears modest white camellia-like flowers only an inch or so across in early summer, smaller and less showy than those of its better-known relative Stewartia pseudocamellia. Its chief garden merit is the smooth, flaking bark that reveals patches of orange, gray, and cream on mature trunks, giving excellent winter interest. Grow it in cool, moist, acidic soil with dappled shade similar to a rhododendron planting, sheltered from drying wind and harsh afternoon sun. It is slow to establish and best suited to woodland gardens and specialty collections rather than a typical foundation planting.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in a sheltered, mild-winter site with fertile, well-drained soil.

directions: Hong Kong dogwood is an evergreen tree from subtropical southern China and Vietnam, holding its glossy, leathery leaves year-round rather than dropping them like the familiar deciduous dogwoods. In late spring it carries flat heads of tiny true flowers surrounded by four to six creamy-white bracts, followed by clusters of fleshy red to purplish compound fruit. It needs a genuinely mild, frost-light climate such as coastal California or the milder parts of the Gulf Coast and is grown as a specimen or screening tree where winters stay well above hard frost. Provide shelter from cold wind and well-drained, fertile soil for best performance.

planting.note: Plant container stock in fall or early spring along streambanks or in seasonally moist foothill soils.

directions: Blackfruit dogwood is a California native shrub or small tree found along streams and in seasonally moist drainages within Sierra Nevada foothill woodlands, often growing beneath blue oak and gray pine. It produces small, inconspicuous yellow-green flower clusters without showy bracts in early spring, followed by distinctive dull black fruit that gives the species its name. Unlike the big-bract dogwoods grown for flower display, this species is valued by native-plant gardeners for streambank stabilization, wildlife food, and naturalistic foothill plantings rather than ornamental bloom. It tolerates summer dry-down once established but performs best with some residual soil moisture near seasonal drainages.
